*2. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether there has been a sharp decline in deposits with the 
scheduled commercial banks;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) No, Sir. Deposits of scheduled 
commercial banks have not recorded any decline. On the contrary, deposits

from Rs.9,62,618 crore as on March 23, 2001 to Rs. 10,78,971 crore as on 
February 8, 2002.

accept/reject the applications depending upon their needs. The main reasons

Scheme and (ii) applications in excess of the assessed surplus. Out of 10,714

subsequently withdrawn. 7314 applications were  accepted which account for 
around 9% of the total staff strength of these banks. All the applications

Economic Growth 
  *7. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY:                   
SHRI RUMAtfDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item captioned 
"Economy grew by just 4 per cent last year" which appeared in the Times of 
India dated the 1st February, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Governme nt declared 5.2 per cent growth of 
economy during 2000-2001 and 6.4 per cent during 1999-2000; 
(d) if so, in what manner it has now been declared only 4 per cent growth and 
how far agricultural and other products were affected during the period; and 
(e) the steps being taken by Government to improve the economy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The said news-item appearing in the Times of India dated February 1, 
2002 states that as per Quick Estimates (QE) released by the Central Statistical 
Organisation (CSO), growth rate of the Indian economy plummeted to a meagre 4 
per cent in 2000-2001 from the previous years 6.1 per cent. Further CSO estimated 
in June last year that the economy had grown by 5.2. per cent in 2000-2001 as 
against 6.4 per cent in 1999-2000. The revision of the growth rate is mainly 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2002] 
 
attributed to a 0.4 per cent decline in agriculture output and 2.2 per cent fall in the 
banking and insurance sector. The negative growth in agriculture was mainly on 
account of decline in production of rice, wheat, pulses, oilseeds and cotton. The 
manufacturing sector grew by a modest 6.7 per cent, construction by 6.8 per 
cent, communication by 15 per cent, real estate and business services by 9 per 
cent and other services grew by. 7.4 per cent. The negative growth of 21.2 per 
eent in banking and insurance sector was mainly because of decline in the output of 
the non-banking financial institutions. 
(c) As per the Revised Estimates of National Income for 2000-2001 released 
by the CSO on June 29,2001 the growth in the gross domestic product (GDP) at 
factor cost (1993-94 prices) was estimated at 6.4 per cent and 5.2 per cent for 
1999-2000 and 2000-2001 respectively. The same has now been estimated at 6.1 
per cent and 4 per cent for 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 respectively as per the QE of 
National Income for 2000-2001 released by the CSO on January 31, 2002. 
(d) This change in the GDP growth estimate for 2000-2001 has been 
necessitated due to downward revision in the production data for foodgrains 
from 199 million tonnes reported in Janua ry, 2001 to 196 million tonnes as of 
now and fall in the output of non-banking financial ins titutions. The downward 
revision in agriculture also led to the cascading effect in terms of lower growth in 
the sectors trade, hotels etc. 
(e) With a view to promoting growth, the broad strategy has been enunciated 
in the Budget speech 2001-2002. The Budget for 2001-2002 has also provided 
enhanced central plan outlays for key infrastructure sectors. Also increased 
emphasis has been placed on accelerating capital investment expenditure. Besides, 
measures have been taken to stimulate domestic demand. These among other 
include reduction in interest rates on contractual savings, tax cuts through 
abolition of surcharge payable by corporates and non-corporates, further scaling 
down of peak customs tariff, major simplification in the excise duty regime etc. 
Further Reserve Ratio of India on the basis of a review of macro- economic and 
monetary developments  reduced   the  bank   rate  of 6.5   per  cent   and  also 
24 

[26 February, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
affected reduction and rationalisation in the Cash Reserve Ratio for the 
banking system. These specific measures to stimulate demand in the 
backdrop of Budget strategy are exp ected to have a favourable impact on 
growth.

India's Share in World Exports 
*10. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that although exports during 2000-2001 rose by 18 
per cent to touch $ 44 billion, yet they were lower than other Asian countries 
like Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor, indicati ng India's present share of world's 
exports; 
(c) whether under new medium-term export strategy, Government would 
be able to achieve the target of annual exports of $ 80 billion by 2007 as 
well as cornering India's share of world exports to 1 per cent; and 
(d) whether tax rebates, export subsidies given by Government 
would stay or India's strategy would be WTO compatible? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) and (b) India's 
exports during 2000-2001 are valued at US $ 44.56 billion as compared to the 
level of US $ 36.82 billion during April-March, 1999-2000 thereby, 
registering a growth of 21% which was higher than the target of 18% set for 
the year 2000-2001. This is the highest export growth rate achieved in the last 
decade. As per WTO International Trade Statistics, the value of exports of 
India for 2000, is lower than that of Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore. The 
21% growth of exports in dollar terms achieved during the year 2000-2001 is 
basically due to the favourable world economic situation, outstanding 
performance by the exporting community and several export promotion 
measures, as enumerated in the EXIM policy. 
(c) Taking Stock of the developments  in the recent past and considering 
the current global economic environment, the Medium Term Export Strategy 
for the period 2002—2007 has been announced. Medium Term Export 
Strategy gives broad directions by giving a road map for export sector by 
setting targets, in the medium term, in order to achieve US $ 80 billion i.e. 
1% of world exports by the year 2007. Key macro policies and sector-wise 
policies have been suggested to reach the target of 1% share which is 
achievable. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2002] 
(d) Our export incentive schemes like Duty Drawback cannot be 
considered as subsidies as they are meant for rebating indirect taxes and 
import duties on the imported inputs to be used for production of export 
products and are WTO compatible.

*14. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) has 
recently been signed between China and India with regard to the Brahmaputra 
river; 
(b) if so, the details and the objectives thereof; and 
(c) what follow-up steps Government propose to take to plan and prepare for 
the floods and also work out water resources development plans in the 
catchment areas as a result of the proposed agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) During the visit of Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji to India in 
January, 2002, an MoU was signed between the Ministry of Water Resources of 
India and Ministry of Water Resources of China on provision of hydrological 
information of the Yaluzangbu/ Brahmaputra river in flood season by China to 
India. As per the MoU, China will provide India with information on water 
level, discharge and rainfall twice a day from June 1 to October 15 each year in 
respect of three hydrological stations—Nugesha, Yangcun and Nuxia—lying on the 
mainstream of the Brahmaputra river. The Chinese side has also agreed to 
provide this hydrological information if water level exceeds mutually agreed 
levels during the non-flood season. China has further agreed to provide 
information on a real time basis on abnormal rise/fall in the water level/discharge 
and other information which might lead to sudden floods on the basis of 
existing monitoring and data collection facilities. The two sides are to conclude an 
Implementation Plan to implement the understanding reached in the MoU. The 
above information will be useful in flood forecasting activities on the downstream of 
Brahmaputra river in India.

Guidelines for recovery of dues rela ting to Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) 
of Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks 
In the recent past, we have been r eceiving representations from urban banks 
and federations of urban banks for issue of guidelines relating to compromise 
settlements of Non-Performance Assets (NPAs). You are aware that there are 
no uniform provisions in the Co-operative Societies Acts/Rules for the Board 
of Directors to enter into compromise settlements with the borrowers in 
respect of any loans gran ted by them and waiver/write off contemplated 
under one time settlement proposals require the approval of the Registrar of 
Co-operative Societies. However, cons idering the increasing trend in NPAs 
of urban banks and the delay in settlement of court cases covering such loans 
and advances, it is felt necessary to is sue guidelines to urban banks for the 
purpose of streamlining the systems and procedures followed by them for one 
time settlements.

not desirable to issue mandatory guidelines as we have done in the

    Draft Guidelines for One Time Settlement (OTS) of Non-Performing 
Assets (NPAs) by Urban Cooperative Banks 
1. Coverage 
The guidelines will apply to all non- performing accounts, in all sectors 
irrespective of the nature of business/activity/purposc of advances, which had 
become doubtful or loss assets as on 31 March 1998. The guidelines will also 
cover NPAs which were classified as sub-standard as on 31 March, 1998, and 
which have subsequently 
82 
 

[26 February, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
become doubtful or loss assets. However, the Registrar of Cooperative 
Societies (RCS) may fix and other cut-off date prior to March 31, if he so 
desires. The following categories of loans will not be covered by the scheme. 
(a) Cases wilful default, frauds and malfeasance. 
(b) Loans with tie-up arrangement for recovery (e.g. loans availed by 
salary earners). 
(c) Loans availed of or guaranteed by Directors or by close relatives of 
Directors or by firms/companies/ins titutions in which the Directors are 
interested or by ex-Directors of respective urban cooperative banks. 
 
(d) Loans guaranteed by Government (including cases where Government 
guarantee has been invoked but not honoured by the Government). 
(e) Loans due from Government Department/Undertakings. 
(f) Loans under Government directed programmes. 
2. Cut-off levels in the NPAs accounts identified as per (i) above 
The RCS should fix the cut-off limit for individual borrowers and institutional 
borrowers (i.e. firms/companies/other institutions), under all loan accounts, 
The cut-off limits may be fixed based on either loans outstanding or working 
capital of the bank or its deposits as on 31 March 2001, as may be decided the 
RCS on the basis of the above norms, say for banks having loans/working 
capital/deposits upto Rs. 25 crore, above Rs. 25 crore but upto Rs. 50 crore 
and so on. There should be a uniform criteria for this purpose. 
3. Settlement formula 
(i) NPAs classified as Doubtful or Loss Assets as on 31 March 1998 
Minimum amount to be recovered : 100 per cent of the outstanding balance 
in the account inclusive of  interest as on the date on which the account was 
categorised as doubtful asset. 
(ii) NPAs classified as Sub-standard as on 31 March 1996 which became 
Doubtful or Loss Assets subsequently 
Minimum amount to be covered : 100 per cent of the outstanding balance in 
the account inclusive of interest as on the date on which the account was 
classified as doubtful plus interest  at a rate not less than the minimum 
lending rate per annum thereafter till the date of final payment. 
83 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2002] 
(iii) Penal interest, other charges and payment of settlement amount in 
instalments 
(i) Penal interest, legal charges and other charges could be waived. 
(ii) Amount of settlement arrived at as above should be recovered preferably 
in one lumpsum. In cases where the bo rrowers arc unable to pay the entire 
amount in one lumpsum, at least 25 pe r cent of the amount of settlement 
should be recovered upfront and the balance amount of 75 per cent recovered 
in instalments within a maximum period of one year togcthcrwith interest at 
minimum lending rate from the date of settlement upto the date of final 
payment. 
4. Competent Authority 
The scheme is to be approved by the Board of Directors of the concerned 
banks within the provision of the Co-operative Societies Act/ 
Rules/Notification/Administrative guidelines issued by the concerned 
Registrar of Co-operative Societies. A Settlement Advisory Committee should 
be constituted by the banks to review all applications received and to 
recommend eligible cases to the Competent Authority for sanction. The 
powers to sanction waiver/ remission of penal interest, charges and to take all 
related decisions may be vested with the Board within the provision of the 
Co-operative Societies Acts /Rules /Notification /Administrative Guidelines 
issued by the concerned RCS. The Scheme will be non-discrctionary and non-
discriminatory. 
5. Non-discretionary and No n-discriminatory treatment 
The banks should follow the guidelines for compromise settlement of all 
NPAs covered, without discrimination among borrowers. The guidelines arc 
non-discrctionary inasmuch as the CEO /Board of Directors should not 
deviate from the parameters indicated in the guidelines for compromise 
settlement of NPAs. 
84 

[26 February, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Operative period of the Scheme 
The Scheme will remain operative upto June 30, 2002. The applications 
received for OTS upto June 30, 2002 should be processed and decisions taken 
thereon at the earliest but not later than September 30, 2002. 
7. Settlement Advisory Committees (SACs) 
(i) Constitution of SACs 
The Board at the Head Office may constitute SAC comprising officials of the 
bank. The Committee may comprise of the Chairman, Directors, Chief Executive 
Officer of the bank, another Senior Official and or a Consultant who has 
experience in the field of banking, management or law. The official who has 
sanctioned the particular loan which has become NPA under his delegated authority 
should not participate in the SAC m eeting where that loan account is under 
consideration for settlement. The SAC constituted as above may review 
requests for compromise settlements from eligible borrowers. 
(ii) Functioning of SAC 
(a) The Boards of banks may draw broad guidelines and procedures for the 
functioning of SAC. SAC may recommend eligible cases for approval of 
compromise settlements within the powers delegated under the Co-operative 
Societies Act / Administrative instructions. Powers for compromise proposals, 
wherever delegated to the Board of Directors of urban banks as per the Co-
operative Societies Act/Rules should be exercised only on the recommendation 
of SAC. 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2002] 
(b) The Board should review the decisions taken by the SAC every month 
and ensure that the process of settlement is complete within the stipulated 
period. 
8. Action against other defaulters 
In cases where restructuring is not f easible or defaulters have not come 
forward for compromise settlement, suits must be filed promptly for recovery 
of dues Banks should follow up suit filed cases vigorously and effectively in 
the Courts to decide the cases and realization of dues at the earliest. 
9. General 
(i) In cases of NPAs where arbitratio n /execution petitions have been filed 
and or degree obtained and recovery certificates issued, the settlement as per 
these guidelines will be with the consent of the Competent Authority. 
(ii) A long term multi-pronged and effective NPA management 
strategy should  be put  in place in  each  institution to arrest the 
incidence of fresh NPAs. 
 
(iii) The waiver that may be allowed by the banks in terms of these 
guidelines will have to be on their own strength and no financial support from 
Government or RBI would be extended. 
(iv) The banks should submit a report on the progress in recovery of NPAs 
under the guidelines every quarter to the Board of Directors. 
(v) A copy of the final guidelines issued by the State Government may be 
sent to us for our information and record.

3. Unlike the public sector banks, cooperatives provide loans and advances 
through on-lending as well as directly to constituents. In the case of loans and 
advances for agriculture and non-farm  activities, the SCBs and DCCBs are 
intermediary agencies engaged in fi nancing Primary Agricultural Credit 
Societies (PACS) for on-lending to ultimate borrowers. Further, bulk of the 
NPAs of DCCBs are under short-term agricultural loans, reflecting the 
overdues/NPAs at the primary level against farmers. DCCBs provide loans 
directly to individuals for various purposes (other than agriculture) and also 
to non-credit cooperative societies engaged in manufacture/ procurement, 
processing, marketing, etc., with or without refinance support from SCBs 
which too provide direct loans to individuals and cooperative societies for 
various purposes. Consequent to the tier system in cooperatives, the terms 
and process of one-time settlement in the case of advance under on-lending 
through primaries/DCCBs will have to be  stipulated at the ultimate borrower 
level and the proceeds of settlement as well as costs and losses arising 
therefrom will have to be shared between the various tiers involved, on a 
mutually agreed basis. 
4. Keeping in view the special characteristics of cooperatives as mentioned 
above, the following guid elines for recovery of chronic NPAs have since 
been finalised by the Reserve Bank of India, as a one-time measure, for 
cooperative credit institutions.

(i) Coverage 
A. SCBs/DCCBs.  
a. NPAs  in  all  sectors irrespective  of the  nature  of business/ 
activity/purpose, which had become doubtful or loss as on 31 March, 
1998. 
b. NPAs which were classified as sub-standard as on 31 March 
1998 and which have subsequently become doubtful or loss 
category. 
B. PACS  
Overdues for three years and more as on 31 March 1998 which had 
become doubtful of recovery. 
C. Cases of wilful default, frauds and malfeasance, loans with tie-up 
arrangement for recovery (e.g. sa lary earners, societies), loans 
availed of and guaranteed by Directors of respective cooperative 
institutions, loans guaranteed by Government (including cases 
where Government guarantee has been invoked but not honoured 
by the Government), loans due from Government Departments/ 
undertakings, loans under Government directed programmes like 
PDS, will not be covered. 
(ii) Cut off levels in the NPAs / overdue, 
accounts identified as per (i) above 
A. SCBs/DCCBs—Outstanding bala nce not to exceed Rs. 5 lakh 
per individual borrower and Rs. 500 lakh per institutional 
borrower, under all loan accounts. 
B. PACS—Outstanding balance not to exceed Rs. 5 lakh per 
borrower under all loan accounts. 
Outstanding balance for the above pu rpose would cover principal and 
normal interest due as on 31 March 1998 [in respect of SCBs/ DCCBs and 
PACS].

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2002] 
(iii) Settlement formula 
A. SCBs/DCCBs  
a. NPAs classified as doubtful or loss as on 31 March 1998: 
Minimum amount to be recovered: 100 per cent of the outstanding balance in the 
account inclusive of interest as on the date on which the account was 
categorised as doubtful NPAs. 
b. NPAs classified as Sub-standard as on 31 March 1998 
which became doubtful or loss subsequently: 
Minimum amount to be recovered: 100 per cent outstanding balance in the 
account inclusive of interest as on the date on which the account was classified 
as doubtful plus interest at minimum lending rate of 12 per cent per annum 
thereafter till the date of final payment. 
B. PACS  
Minimum amount to be recovered: 100 per cent of the balance outstanding 
[inclusive of interest] when the account became overdue for 3 years.

instalments 
a. Penal interest, legal charges and other charges may be waived. 
b. Amount of settlement arrived at as above, should be recovered 
preferably in one lumpsum. In cas es where the borrowers are unable 
to pay the entire amount in one lumpsum, atleast 25% of the amount 
of settlement should be recovered upfront and the balance amount of 
75 per cent recovered in instalments within a maximum period of one 
year together with interest at minimum lending rate i.e. 12% p.a. 
from the date of settlement upto the date of final payment.

Impact of Euro Currencies on Indian Economy 
97. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state the like ly effect of the introduction of 
Euro currencies on the Indian curre ncies and its overall impact on the 
Indian economy according to the analysis made by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): European countries in the Euro-currency 
area account for a major share in India's trade and investment. The major 
positive implication of Euro on business is the reduction in transaction costs 
and elimination of exchange rate uncertainty. With the introduction of a 
common currency, the Indian importers and exporters may benefit as they 
have to hedge risk only in one currency, the Euro, instead of multiple 
currencies. This will clearly reduce their costs of risk monitoring and 
hedging. Importers will benefit from being able to compare prices more easily 
between eurozone countries and select on price. Exporters will have to 
harmonise selling prices in different markets. Travellers to eurozone will 
save exchange in costs associated with conversion and reconversion of the 
national currencies. Indian companies wi ll be able to enter one coherent 
market free from impediments to intern al trade with an impressive growth 
potential.'Selecting a business location in Europe will be easier for Indian 
companies as exchange rate considerations no longer matter for the choice of 
the right business location.

Resources; 
(b) if so, the details of the deliberations and decisions taken by the 
working group; 
(c) whether the draft National Water Policy is likely to be revised in the 
light of the recommendations of the working group; and 
(d) by when the National Policy Guidelines for water allocation is likely 
to be put in place? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Two 
meetings of the Working Group of the National Water Resources Council 
(NWRC) were held on 22nd May, 2001 and 24th September, 2001 under the 
Chairmanship of Minister of Water Resources wherein the views of the various 
States on the draft National Water Policy were considered. The provisions 
regarding setting up of river Basin organizations, water allocation amongst 
the States, ecological needs of the rivers inter alia were discussed. Keeping in 
view these deliberations, certain modifications have been carried out in the 
proposed draft policy. In the last (second) meeting of the Working Group, the 
members, after detailed discussions, arrived at a near consensus on the draft 
National Water Policy which has been recommended for adoption by the 
National Water Resources Council. The draft National Water Policy will be 
considered by the National Water Resources Council in its next meeting to be 
held shortly for its adoption. 
(d) In so far as the draft National Policy Guidelines for Water Allocation 
amongst the States are concerned, the Working Group

has recommended for referring them to the National Water Board of NWRC for 
having a re-look and arriving at a consensus. 
Districts affected by ground water contamination 
155. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of districts which are affected by ground water contamination 
like arsenic and fluorosis, State-wise; and 
(b) the total amount of money earmarked for containing the menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) A statement 
indicating names of States and Districts where ground water has been found 
contaminated with arsenic and fluoride is enclosed. (See below) 
(b) The provision of drinking water supply is the responsibility of the State 
Governments. Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments and provides financial assistance under the Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). 
Under ARWSP, upto 20% of the allotted funds can be utilised to tackle water 
quality problems. In such quality affected areas, where ground water is unfit for 
drinking, the safe drinking water is supplied either through alternative sources, 
tapping surface water or treatment of  quality problems through suitable 
removal unit. In urban areas, the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation assists the States for the provisions of safe drinking water. 
The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) also provides technical services to the 
State Governments. The CGWB undertakes periodic monitoring of water quality. 
The data thus collected is made available to concerned State agencies. The 
Board has sanctioned funds amounting to Rs. 59.78 lakh to the Government of 
West Bengal to study arsenic contamination in ground water in the State.
